fixes.explanation: Seven is a fair guess, friend, but the count here runs bigger. God asks for “…twelve staffs, one from the leader of each tribe.” (Numbers 17:2) Moses ends up with “…twelve staffs in all.” (Numbers 17:6) Stopping at seven is like counting a tray of cookies and walking off halfway down the rows.

Careful, friend, because this one is True. God tells Moses, “Write each man’s name on his staff…” (Numbers 17:2) Each leader gets his own name on his own staff. It's like writing your name on your charger at work, so nobody walks off with it and acts surprised.

That's the one, baker. Levi is a tribe too, so it gets a staff, and God says “…write Aaron’s name on the staff of Levi…” (Numbers 17:3) The reason He gives is “…there must be one staff for the head of each tribe.” Nobody gets a blank staff in this lineup.

Eleazar is a name you might know, friend, but this verse doesn't use it. God says, “…write Aaron’s name on the staff of Levi…” (Numbers 17:3) His reason is that “…there must be one staff for the head of each tribe.” So the name going on Levi's staff comes straight from God's instructions, and it's Aaron's.

All of it, baker! Moses walks in the next day and sees that Aaron's staff “…had sprouted, put forth buds, blossomed, and produced almonds.” (Numbers 17:8) Most of us come back the next day to a pile of emails. Moses came back to a staff covered in buds, blossoms and almonds.

Priests is a fair guess, friend, but it isn't the word God uses here. He says the staff is to be “…kept as a sign for the rebellious…” (Numbers 17:10) He gives the purpose too: “…so that you may put an end to their grumbling against Me, lest they die.” The blank is for the rebellious.
